Primary strength — pop: Board has explosive, springboard-like pop; carbon stringers provide approximately 15% extra pop over standard Artifact [47] 98. Ride feel: Lively, tried-and-true camber park board with predictable, intuitive turning [48] 99. Press/butter performance: Double Kick nose and tail create a "cheat code" extra leverage point for locking into tall, stylish-looking presses [48][49] 100. Carving ability: Predictable, balanced, consistent — best for medium-radius turns at casual speeds; no "wow moments" for carving [48] 101. Switch riding: Excellent — centered true twin excels for switch riding [50] 102. Spin ability: Good for spins — feels balanced and easy to spin in the air [50] 103. Jib performance: Decent on jibs; approach and dismount are good but some reviewers found it not amazing while actually on the rail/box [50] 104. Edge hold: Full camber provides strong edge hold; margin for error smaller than hybrid camber boards [25] 105. Speed stability: Can handle a good amount of speed before instability, but there is a limit [50] 106. Powder performance: Likely woeful in powder — full camber, true twin, zero setback all work against powder float [51][52] 107. Weight (on scales): Pretty close to average weight; slightly under average based on sample of ~250 models weighed [53] 108. User experience — lightness: Described as "super light weight" enabling easy rotations [54] 109. Camber height (measured, 2024 model): 6.5mm at highest point (reviewer-measured, unweighted) [55] 110. Camber height — disagreement: A reader/owner claimed Artifact boards have super low camber (~2–3mm); reviewer measured 6.5mm; variance debated [55][56] 111. Break-in required: Board requires a break-in period to dial in; performance improves after several days of riding [57] 112. Base speed when waxed: Noticeably fast — same SinterStrong base used in Rome Ravine [58] 113. Base speed when dry: Noticeably slow — requires regular waxing to maintain speed [58] 114. Base maintenance requirement: Higher than extruded base; needs waxing to maintain above-average glide [58] 115. Whitelines 100 selection (2023–2024): Selected again for Whitelines top 100 snowboard products [25] 117. Negative review — top coat durability: "Only complaint is the top coat durability but that's the downside of a board this light" [67] 129. Positive warranty experience (Rome Artifact/Mechanic): Rome replaced a warranty-issue board quickly with "excellent customer service" [68] 130. Review summary on Rome US: 15 reviews; 67% 5-star, 20% 4-star, 7% 2-star, 7% 1-star [41] 131. Warranty (US): 2-year limited warranty against manufacturing defects from date of purchase from Authorized Dealer [69] 132. Extended warranty: 2+1 year warranty — register product within 12 months and subscribe to newsletter for 3rd year [70] 133. Warranty (EU): 3-year limited guarantee against manufacturing defects [71] 134. Warranty coverage includes: Delamination, insert problems, cracked topsheet (outside binding area, if wood core not broken) [69] 135. Warranty exclusions: Impact damage, natural wear and tear, negligence [71] 136. Return policy (Rome direct): 45-day return period [72] 137. Flex rating (Rome, evo, most retailers): 5/10 [1][38][73] 138. Flex rating (Powderstuff.com): 6/10 (medium-stiff) [74] — DISAGREEMENT: One source rates flex at 6/10 vs manufacturer's 5/10. Manufacturer rating of 5/10 is far more widely corroborated and should be trusted. 139. Comparable product: CAPiTA DOA — hybrid camber (more forgiving), slightly more expensive (~$20 more) [27] 140. CAPiTA DOA vs Artifact Pro — camber: DOA uses hybrid camber (catch-free zones in nose/tail), Artifact Pro has traditional full camber [27] 141. CAPiTA DOA vs Artifact Pro — forgivingness: DOA more forgiving for learning tricks and off-axis landings [27] 142. CAPiTA DOA vs Artifact Pro — pressability: Artifact Pro is noticeably easier to press thanks to Double Kick [27] 143. Comparable product: CAPiTA Ultrafear — stiffer freestyle twin for park durability and serious pop [74] 144. Comparable product: Nitro T1 — classic park twin with strength and pop for heavy freestyle sessions [74] 145. Comparable product: Bataleon Evil Twin — more stability and all-mountain park power, still freestyle at heart (flex 6/10) [74] 146. Comparable in-brand: Rome Agent — similar flex rating, camrock vs full camber profile; Agent has softer flex and better butterability [75] 147. Rome Agent Pro 2027: Fusion Camber, flex 7/10, stiffer and more all-mountain focused, $606 USD at S2AS [76] 148. Rome Artifact (non-Pro): Softer (flex ~4/10), extruded PowerSlide base, bamboo hotrods instead of carbon [77][78] 149. Rider level: Advanced [1] — merchant verified 150. Target rider (Board of the World): Intermediate to advanced park rider looking to progress skills [48] 151. Not suitable for: Complete beginners — camber profile too unforgiving; not catch-free [79][48] 152. Not suitable for: High-speed resort carving — too lively; features better suited to jumping/jibbing [80] 153. Best use case: Park laps, side hits, urban riding, freestyle-focused riding [11] 154. One-board quiver potential: Can work as a one-board quiver if you don't ride powder [51] 155. Two-board quiver pairing: Pairs well with a powder-oriented board for a balanced quiver [51] 156. Construction layup order (bottom to top): SinterStrong Base → Biax Lower Glass → Carbon HotRod → Pop Core → Biax Upper Glass → Topsheet [41] 157. Sidewall construction (2027): FlaxWalls — flax-reinforced sidewalls for vibration dampening [11] 158. Binding compatibility: Compatible with any binding using standard or mini disc (2x4 pattern) [81] 159. Insert configuration: 2x4 pattern allows for fine-tuned stance positioning [81] 160. Riding style: Park, freestyle, urban, street missions [38] 161. Nose/tail design: Rounded popsicle-stick shape (2026+), traditional pill shape with Double Kick [19] 162. Torsional flex: Biax glass makes torsional flex playful and easy to manipulate [45] 163. Longitudinal pop: Carbon HotRods sit underneath binding inserts for ollie boost while keeping waist bendy [82] 164. Impact absorption: Flax Impact Plates use natural shock-absorbing properties of flax fibres [83] 165. Flax fibre properties: Tough and naturally shock-absorbing [83] 166. Directional flex: Not directional — symmetric flex pattern (true twin) [38] 167. Manufacturing location: Unverified — not explicitly stated on manufacturer site (common for snowboard brands to manufacture in Austria, China, or UAE-based facilities) 168.
